Sinclair SSM × NASA POWER: LT Soybean Water Use Analysis

RIG Project 2024-2026 · PI: Elvis F. Elli

2026-05-20

1 Project Overview

1.1 Background

The limited-transpiration (LT) trait in soybean restricts stomatal conductance under high vapour-pressure deficit (VPD), reducing water loss during the hottest parts of the day. In rain-fed production systems — particularly in the southern United States — this trait is hypothesised to conserve soil water early in the season and redistribute it toward the critical grain-filling period, ultimately protecting yield under drought stress.

This report synthesises output from the Sinclair Soybean Model (SSM), a process-based crop model driven by observed daily weather, with NASA POWER-derived reference evapotranspiration (ETo, Penman–Monteith FAO-56) to evaluate how the LT trait alters seasonal water use and crop coefficients across a wide range of environments.

1.2 Experimental Design

Factor Levels
Genotype Non-limited transpiration (check), Limited transpiration (LT)
Water management Rainfed, Irrigated
State AR (Arkansas), MO (Missouri), NE (Nebraska)
Locations Jonesboro, Marianna (AR); Columbia, Norborne (MO); Lincoln, North Platte (NE)
Years simulated 1990 – 2019 (30 years)
Total simulation units 2160

The SSM was run for two genotypes × two water-management scenarios × six locations × 30 years, yielding 2 160 simulation-years of seasonal crop ET (SUMETT), yield, and phenological data. NASA POWER provided daily weather inputs and was used independently to compute growing-season ETo (DOY 120 – 300) for crop-coefficient analysis.

4 Marin-Style Daily ETc vs ETo Scatter

Inspired by Marin et al. (2016, 2019), we compute daily proxies from seasonal totals:

  • ETc_daily = SUMETT ÷ R7.PM (mean daily crop ET over the season, mm/day)
  • ETo_daily = ETo_season_mm ÷ 181 (mean daily reference ET over DOY 120–300, mm/day)

The regression slope of ETc ~ ETo gives an effective seasonal Kc. A slope < 1 indicates that crop ET increases more slowly than atmospheric demand — the signature of stomatal down-regulation documented by Marin et al. for coupled crops.

Figure 4. Marin-style scatter of mean daily crop ET vs mean daily ETo. Each point is one simulation-year. Lines are OLS regressions; slope = effective seasonal Kc. Facets show the four genotype <U+00D7> water-management combinations.

5 Crop Coefficient (Kc) Analysis

The crop coefficient is computed for each simulation-year as:

\[K_c = \frac{\text{SUMETT}}{\text{ETo\_season\_mm}}\]

This integrates across all crop growth stages and is compared to the FAO-56 mid-season Kc benchmark of 1.15 for soybean.

Figure 5. Seasonal crop coefficient (Kc = SUMETT / ETo_season_mm) by genotype, state, and water management. Red dashed line marks the FAO-56 mid-season Kc = 1.15.

Key observation: Kc values consistently fall below the FAO-56 benchmark of 1.15 across all states and management scenarios, consistent with the sub-unity effective Kc reported by Marin et al. (2019) for soybean when accounting for the full growing season. The LT genotype shows systematically lower Kc under rain-fed conditions, reflecting stomatal restriction under high-VPD demand.

7 Water Productivity

Water productivity (WP) is defined as grain yield per unit of seasonal crop ET:

\[WP = \frac{\text{Yield (kg/ha)}}{\text{SUMETT (mm)}} \quad [\text{kg ha}^{-1} \text{mm}^{-1}]\]

Higher WP indicates more grain produced per unit of water transpired — a key metric for evaluating the agronomic value of the LT trait.

8 Map: Yield Outcomes Across Sites

Figure 9. Spatial distribution of simulated soybean yields across the six study locations. Source: figures/Fig_map_yields_facet.png.

The six study locations span a broad agroclimatic gradient from the humid Lower Mississippi Delta (Jonesboro and Marianna, AR) northward through the Corn Belt (Columbia and Norborne, MO) to the semi-arid Great Plains (Lincoln and North Platte, NE). This gradient captures a wide range of seasonal ETo (ca. 550–850 mm) and rainfall regimes, making the dataset particularly well-suited to evaluating the LT trait’s context-dependency.

9 Marin et al. Insights: The Kc–ETo Inverse Relationship

9.1 The Core Finding

Marin et al. (2016) (Agric. Water Manage. 163: 139–145) were among the first to document systematically that crop coefficients decrease as reference evapotranspiration increases for “coupled” canopies — that is, crops whose stomata respond to atmospheric demand. Using maize and soybean data from Brazil, they showed that:

“At high ETo, the ratio ETc/ETo decreases because stomatal resistance increases faster than the Penman–Monteith aerodynamic term alone predicts.”

Their 2019 follow-up (Marin et al., Theor. Appl. Climatol. 138: 1785–1793) confirmed that a whole-season Kc of ~0.83 for soybean was more appropriate than the FAO-56 value of 1.15, particularly when ETo was high, because the standard approach assumes a decoupled (well-watered, non-stomata-limited) crop.

9.2 Connection to the LT Trait

The LT soybean genotype amplifies this inverse relationship:

  1. Stomatal restriction: Under high VPD (which co-occurs with high ETo), LT genotypes close stomata earlier in the day, decoupling crop ET from atmospheric demand even more strongly than standard genotypes.

  2. Kc suppression: As shown in Section 5 of this report, LT plants consistently show lower Kc values than non-LT plants under rain-fed conditions, where VPD-driven demand is met largely from soil water reserves.

  3. Water conservation: Because LT genotypes use less water per unit ETo at high-demand moments, they retain more soil water for grain filling — the key mechanism behind yield protection under terminal drought.

  4. Irrigated dampening: Under irrigation, the LT advantage diminishes because water supply keeps pace with demand, reducing the selection pressure for stomatal restriction.

9.3 Implications for FAO-56 Parameterisation

De Melo et al. (2026) (Agronomy J.) argue that the FAO-56 framework systematically overestimates soybean ETc in high-ETo environments because:

  • The tabulated Kc = 1.15 assumes full canopy with no stomatal downregulation.
  • Plant-available water (PAW) assumptions do not account for the partial stomatal closure that occurs well above the theoretical wilting point.
  • LT genotypes effectively shift the ETc–ETo relationship toward a lower and flatter slope — behaviour that is invisible to standard Kc tables.

Practical consequence: Irrigation scheduling based on FAO-56 with Kc = 1.15 will systematically over-irrigate soybean (especially LT cultivars) in environments where ETo > 5 mm/day. The Marin-style scatter plots in Section 4 provide an empirical, site-specific recalibration framework directly applicable to each of the six locations simulated here.
